hypothesis: A per-tile cost model fitted to board-measured layer parts predicts the NPU time of a conformer encoder at any length.
prediction: NPU(T) = 16 * (10 us * Tp + b * Tp^2 + 0.025 ms * (2n + n^2)) + 0.048 ms * Tp + 2.1 ms (front end on the CPU), with padded length Tp = n N, n = ceil(T / N), and b between 45 and 67 ns per query-key pair. Per layer the per-frame parts cost 10 to 12.6 us a frame (two feed-forwards 7.2, four projections 1.8, convolution module 3.6 measured alone; the sum of separately measured parts is 7% above the whole layer because the compiler overlaps neighbouring operations, which a tile graph of one part loses); the model uses 10, the fit to the whole layers. The attention core costs 40 ns per query-key pair for all four heads when the block sits in VIP SRAM (the 92-frame layer) and 67 ns per pair in the 64-row blocks at 368 frames. The CPU path is 109.6 ms at 92 frames; scaled linearly (a lower bound) it is 1.19 ms a frame.
conclusion: Tile size N = 128 is the choice: overhead is 3% or less, the score tensor (4 x 128 x 128) and the flat positional tensor (32,640) stay in VIP SRAM and under the 16-bit limit, and padding waste averages 64 frames. N = 256 saves little more and its flat positional tensor, 4 x 256 x 511 = 130,816, exceeds the 16-bit limit unless the gather is reshaped. Beyond about 400 frames the quadratic attention work sets the time: at 500 frames the attention core is 70% of NPU time. For comparison the fixed 92-frame graph set takes 24.6 ms at 92 frames (4.5 times the CPU path), faster than any tile size because it has no padding to 128 and no per-job overhead beyond 18 jobs; it may stay as a fast path for short segments.

Where per-job overhead dominates: **Where the per-job overhead dominates.** An attention step does N^2 x 45 ns of work: 0.046 ms for N = 32 (the 0.025 ms overhead is 35% of the job), 0.18 ms for N = 64 (12%), 0.74 ms for N = 128 (3%), 2.9 ms for N = 256 (1%). A per-frame job of N frames does 10 us x N: the overhead is 7% at N = 32, 4% at 64, 2% at 128. The overhead as a share of the whole segment at 500 frames is 115 ms of 413 for N = 32, 32 ms of 329 for N = 64, 9.6 ms of 307 for N = 128 and 3 ms of 301 for N = 256. **N = 128 is the choice**: the overhead is 3% or less, the score tensor (4 x 128 x 128) and the flat positional

CPU-merge alternative estimate: per layer and tile pair 4 x N x 44 multiply-accumulates, 22,500 for N = 128, about 0.8 ms per layer at 500 frames (an estimate, not measured), 13 ms over 16 layers, about 4% of the NPU time.

hypothesis: The tiled encoder through the copy-per-job queue takes the composed time at 100, 250 and 498 frames.
conclusion: The tiled encoder's time at 100, 250 and 498 frames is 44.9, 117 and 345 ms, composed from board-measured per-job times, not an end-to-end run; no board entry holds them. The four tile graphs at tile 128 take 752.5, 217.8, 177.3 and 320.2 microseconds per job, multiplied by the job count, plus subsampling and head. The whole-clip CPU path takes 118, 255 and 585 ms at the same lengths, but that is whole recognition (front end, encoder and decode), so the columns are not comparable. The word error rate on held-out utterances of 90 to 130 encoder frames, outside the calibration sets, equals the float encoder's, 5.63%; it comes from running every graph in the SDK simulator, not from the board.

hypothesis: One mask value and one initial running maximum can serve all 16 layers of the attention step.
conclusion: They cannot. The score range of the last layer (about -515 to 661, against near zero in the first layers): with the first layer's values a padded key (a zero key row, scoring up to +131) won the maximum, the exponentials of the valid keys underflowed to zero, and the encoder output at 100 frames had cosine 0.940 with float. With per-layer constants derived from the layer's score statistics (largest padded-key score, smallest row maximum over valid keys, lowest valid score), declared in a manifest beside the five graphs of the layer and host-checked (every masked padded key at least 25 below the smallest valid row maximum), the output at 100 frames has cosine 0.9998.

hypothesis: The carried-state attention step in 16-bit dynamic fixed point matches float full attention to about 1% relative RMS error when the calibrated ranges cover the data.
conclusion: The step graph in float equals full attention to 1e-7. In the simulator over every tile pair of one real layer, carrying the state as the simulator returned it: 1% relative RMS error at 500 frames when ranges cover the data. The seven bad head-rows of the second case have a largest score of 20 to 22 while that calibration (largest score 16.3) clipped at 16, a range limit of the calibration, not of the form; production calibration uses many utterances with headroom. The resolution that matters is the row sum l (range 512 when it must reach 500 keys, step 0.016), which costs accuracy on rows whose softmax is concentrated on one key; carrying l/64 would reduce that. The maximum of negative values is kept by compiler, simulator and hardware (docs/hardware/npu-command-formats.md, 'Maximum of negative values'). The step has nine inputs and three outputs, more than the loader's default of eight tensors, so qu and qv travel as one tensor of eight heads.

hypothesis: The attention step for four heads and 128 query rows can run in under 600 microseconds on the board.
prediction: The attention step was required to meet 600 microseconds.
conclusion: Board, one slot, 852 MHz and 800 mV: the step runs as two jobs of 64 query rows against the 128 keys of a tile, 229.4 microseconds each, 458.8 for the step, outputs equal to the simulator byte for byte. The first form with the gather that aligns relative-position scores took about 1.1 ms; aligning by slices took 902 microseconds; the best single-job form with the native softmax took 859. Reformulation facts: the activation unit computes Elu and Elu(x) + 1 equals exp(x) for x at or below zero (the shader's exponential cost 88 microseconds more in a 64-row job); a product with a column of ones appended to the values returns the row sum with the weighted values and a reciprocal of the small row-sum tensor replaces the shader's division; when tensors live at one time exceed the 512 KiB of on-chip memory the same operations cost several times as much (a job of 128 rows takes 731 microseconds, not 459). Over the nine tile pairs of 294 frames of the last layer the form has 1.2% RMS error of the signal, against 4.7% for the shader form on the same calibration. The forms and every timing are in the mimus repository (docs/npu-encoder-offload.md, section 8). The attention step series entries are in docs/evidence/npu.jsonl.

hypothesis: The proposed EL1 rebinding service keeps every job inside its registered regions.
prediction:
Negative tests (host, with the real runtime and service as in `checks/os-npu-service.c`): an offset one byte past the region is refused
and the command stream is byte-for-byte unchanged; an offset that overflows 64 bits is refused; a region of another queue is refused;
an output window overlapping the output window of an unfinished job is refused; a rewrite for a handle with a job in flight is
refused, and after that job completes the rewrite succeeds; a binding that names a region the application then unregisters leaves
no job able to reach it. Board: one job with an address one page past its region faults with an NPU MMU exception and the next job
is correct (as the existing fault tests).
conclusion: Not run: the rebinding calls and service do not exist. The tile graphs ran through the copy-per-job queue instead; the proof plan on one real layer at 100, 250 and 500 frames compared each tile graph with its simulator output, the tiled layer composed from simulator outputs against the untiled graph and against float (byte equality with the untiled graph is not expected, because the tile graphs quantize their intermediates at different points; cosine, mean and maximum error are reported), and job times against the cost model.
narrative: Subsampling graphs named for 32, 64 and 128 were timed on the board at 2.2, 3.7 and 8.7 ms; none compared with the schedule's other costs. The share of copies in the step time is not measured. Proof-plan risk: step numerics (exponentials, running maximum, rescale in 16-bit fixed point); fallback is the CPU merge with the step returning block-local o, m, l. Pool: a compiled set needs an NPU pool of 24 MiB or more for the subsampling graphs; an 8 MiB pool refuses the reservation.
